stops.name: Rome — De Officiis, a father's last book
stops.campa: Even as the Philippics escalate, Cicero finds time to write De Officiis, three books on moral duty addressed to his son Marcus, studying at Athens and, Cicero worries, drinking more than he studies. It becomes his last completed work and his clearest statement of what a life owed to the republic should look like: that nothing base can ever truly be expedient, that no gain is worth the wrong of taking from one man to give to another. He sends it east not knowing it will outlive every regime he has fought to save, copied and argued over for two thousand years after Rome itself has fallen.

stops.name: Rome — the war of the Philippics
stops.campa: Through the winter Cicero delivers Philippic after Philippic, fourteen in all, driving the Senate to declare Antony a public enemy and to back the young Octavian, Caesar's heir, as a counterweight against him, a wager Cicero believes he can manage and later, too late, discovers he cannot. He speaks now almost daily, at nearly sixty, with the same reckless candor as in his consulship and four decades of political memory behind it, staking everything on the belief that the republic, badly wounded, is still worth this last unequal fight against a soldier with legions and no such scruples.
stops.quote: Quis tum nobis, quis populo Romano optulit hunc divinum adulescentem deus? — What god was it who then gave us, who gave the Roman people, this divine young man?

stops.name: Rome — the Second Triumvirate, the proscription
stops.campa: Octavian, Antony, and Lepidus meet near Bononia, patch up their rivalry, and form a triumvirate with absolute power, sealed at once by a proscription list of enemies to be killed without trial and their property seized. Antony, unforgiving of the Philippics, insists on Cicero's name; Octavian, who owes Cicero his very political start, is said to argue two days before yielding him up in exchange for an uncle of Antony's own the young man wants dead. Cicero's name goes onto the list with his brother Quintus and his nephew, and the household begins, too late, to run.

stops.name: Formiae — the flight ends, the death
stops.campa: Cicero is carried in a litter toward the coast at Caieta, meaning to take ship at last for Macedonia and Brutus, but turns back to his villa at Formiae, worn out and telling his slaves to let happen what the gods will. The centurion Herennius and the tribune Popillius, once defended by Cicero himself in a parricide case, find him there and force the litter-bearers to set it down. Cicero pushes his head out toward the swords himself, sparing his men further struggle, and speaks the last words the tradition preserves of the greatest voice Rome ever produced.
stops.quote: There is nothing proper about what you are doing, soldier, but do try to kill me properly.
stops.quote_source: Reported by Plutarch, Life of Cicero 48

stops.name: Rome, the Rostra — the head and hands, Fulvia's needle
stops.campa: Herennius carries the severed head and, on Antony's order, the right hand that wrote the Philippics back to Rome. Antony has them nailed up on the Rostra itself, the platform from which Cicero had spoken against Catiline, against the triumvirs' predecessors, against Antony's own edicts, so that his silence now stands exactly where his voice once had. Fulvia, Antony's wife and Clodius's widow before him, is said to take the head into her lap, spit on it, pull out the tongue, and pierce it through and through with the pins from her own hair, before it is set up for Rome to see.
